strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. The paper addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: test-time adaptation of open-vocabulary vision-language object detectors.

The proposed combination is intuitive and detection-specific. IoU-weighted entropy exploits spatial redundancy among proposals, while image-conditioned prompt selection addresses the observed weakness of uniform prompt averaging.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering YOLO-World and Grounding DINO, multiple model sizes, six natural-shift datasets, and PASCAL-C/COCO-C corruptions. Improvements are consistent across most settings and across mAP, AP50, and AP75.
Comparisons include prompt tuning, visual prompt tuning, DPE, and a parameter-matched adapter baseline. VLOD-TTA improves over the strong adapter baseline, rather than only over zero-shot inference.

The appendix provides useful analyses of hyperparameters, proposal count, adapter placement, prompt construction, batch size, augmentations, pre-adaptation fine-tuning, computational cost, and qualitative behavior. The reported 20 FPS versus 22 FPS for the adapter baseline suggests moderate incremental overhead.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper acknowledges an important limitation of overlap-based weighting for small, low-overlap objects.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol does not explain how hyperparameters were selected without labeled target data. Sensitivity studies are conducted on the same target datasets used for reporting, while key settings differ by detector. A source-only validation protocol or cross-dataset hyperparameter transfer experiment is needed to rule out target-label-informed tuning.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the optimizer, learning rate, score and post-processing thresholds, exact baseline optimization settings, GPT model and prompt-generation instruction, and treatment of discrete top-prompt selection during optimization are not specified. The abstract's code field is blank.

The two claimed components are not isolated in a clean factorial ablation across representative shifts and both detectors. The gamma and lambda sensitivity plots partly reveal their effects, and prompt selection is separately compared with averaging, but results for standard entropy, IWE only, IPS only, and IWE+IPS under identical adaptation settings should be tabulated.

The central reliability assumption is heuristic: connected-component size can reflect anchor/proposal density and object scale rather than correctness, can merge nearby same-class instances through transitive IoU links, and systematically discounts small objects. The driving results and stated Cityscapes limitation expose this issue, but analyses stratified by object size/crowding are absent.

The entropy formulation uses a categorical softmax over requested classes without discussing background proposals or detector-specific score semantics. This is nontrivial because YOLO-World and Grounding DINO do not share an identical probabilistic output model; the paper should clarify exactly which logits and proposals enter the loss for each detector.

Most natural-domain gains over the adapter baseline are modest, no uncertainty or repeated-run statistics are reported, and the strongest corruption evidence is concentrated on YOLO-World. These issues make the otherwise consistent empirical case slightly short of fully convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and comparatively underexplored problem: test-time adaptation of open-vocabulary vision-language object detectors.

The evaluation covers varied shifts, including artistic domains, driving scenes, low light, and common corruptions, and includes both YOLO-World and Grounding DINO. The reported improvements over zero-shot inference are broadly consistent.
The proposed components are intuitive and detection-oriented: IWE exploits spatial agreement among dense proposals, while IPS accounts for prompt sensitivity at the image level.

The appendix includes useful sensitivity, backbone, augmentation, throughput, and corruption-severity analyses. Resetting the adapted parameters after each image also clearly defines the single-image adaptation setting.
weaknesses: The central empirical attribution is inadequate. There is no clear factorial ablation comparing Adapter, Adapter+IWE, Adapter+IPS, and Adapter+IWE+IPS across the main datasets and both detectors. The prompt-only analysis and separate hyperparameter curves do not establish which component causes the reported gains or whether their combination is complementary.

Hyperparameter selection appears to use the evaluation domains themselves. Adapter placement and several settings are chosen from results on Watercolor, ClipArt, and Comic, while the paper acknowledges dataset-dependent optimal IoU thresholds. No validation protocol or label-free selection rule is given, and even the final value of the IoU threshold is not stated. This creates a substantial risk of target-test-set tuning.

Reproducibility is poor despite the extensive appendix. The manuscript omits essential details such as optimizer, learning rate, exact adaptation update, score and NMS thresholds, complete prompt-generation procedure/model, random seeds, and dataset splits. The abstract's code field is empty.

The mathematical formulation does not map convincingly onto the evaluated detectors. It models both systems as normalized region-text cosine classifiers with a categorical softmax, but YOLO-World and Grounding DINO have materially different scoring, objectness/background handling, calibration, and language-conditioned detection mechanisms. The paper does not explain how actual logits are extracted, normalized, or fused across Eq. 5. Entropy over foreground classes without an explicit background/objectness treatment could also sharpen background proposals into false positives.

IPS ranks every class's prompts using the mean similarity over all retained proposals. This statistic can be dominated by background regions, proposal density, or large objects, and it is not object-conditioned. No analysis demonstrates that selected prompts are semantically correct or robust to images in which a class is absent.

IWE uses connected-component size rather than direct local affinity, despite being described as IoU-weighted entropy. Transitive connections can merge separate instances or spatially extended chains of boxes, while small or isolated true objects are explicitly downweighted. The driving results already expose this limitation, but there is little analysis by object size, crowding, or instance count.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. The classification-oriented baselines are custom adaptations whose tuning and parameter budgets differ, while detection-specific TTA methods discussed in related work are not empirically compared. It is therefore unclear whether the margins reflect the objectives or implementation choices.

Many gains over the strongest Adapter baseline are modest, yet results are reported without multiple runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. This is particularly problematic for per-image optimization and generated prompt pools, where implementation variability may be meaningful.

The novelty is limited: the method combines entropy minimization, lightweight adapters, connected-component proposal weighting, and top-ranked prompt ensembling. Given the missing causal ablations and protocol ambiguities, the current evidence does not support the strong claim of a robust general framework.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relatively underexplored problem: test-time adaptation of vision-language object detectors. The combination of IoU-weighted entropy and image-conditioned prompt selection is intuitive, detection-specific, and technically straightforward to integrate with different detector families.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. Results span style shifts, autonomous-driving datasets, low-light imagery, PASCAL-C and COCO-C corruptions, two substantially different VLOD architectures, and additional larger backbones. Improvements are generally consistent across mAP, AP50, and AP75, rather than being confined to one metric or domain.

The proposed method consistently improves over zero-shot inference and the adapted TPT, VPT, DPE, and standard adapter-tuning baselines. Particularly convincing are the gains on stylized datasets and the improvement over zero-shot performance across every reported COCO-C corruption and severity.

The paper includes useful sensitivity analyses for the IoU threshold, cluster exponent, fusion coefficient, prompt-selection fraction, proposal count, batch size, augmentations, adapter placement, and pre-adaptation fine-tuning. It also reports computational overhead: 20 FPS versus 22 FPS for standard adapter tuning and 89 FPS without adaptation, with only 1.61M trainable parameters.

The presentation is clear, with helpful motivation figures, a well-defined one-step per-image adaptation protocol, qualitative examples, and an explicit discussion of the limitation on small, low-overlap objects.
weaknesses: The most important missing experiment is a controlled factorial ablation of IWE and IPS. Prompt selection and hyperparameter plots provide partial evidence, but the paper does not clearly report, under an identical adapter and optimization configuration, standard entropy, IWE alone, IPS alone, and IWE+IPS across both detectors. Consequently, it is difficult to determine how much each claimed contribution accounts for the final gains or whether their effects are complementary.

The model-selection protocol is insufficiently specified and may allow target-test tuning. Adapter placement is chosen using performance on Watercolor, ClipArt, and Comic, and several hyperparameters are analyzed on those same target datasets, but no held-out validation protocol or label-free selection rule is described. This is particularly important for an unsupervised TTA claim, where target annotations should not guide configuration choices.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The manuscript does not specify the optimizer, learning rate, default IoU threshold, detection thresholds, hardware used for FPS, repeated-run variability, or sufficiently detailed baseline hyperparameters. The abstract's code field is blank, and the GPT model, generation instruction, and complete prompt pools are not supplied. The severity or aggregation convention behind the main PASCAL-C tables is also unclear.

The technical novelty is useful but moderate. IWE is essentially entropy reweighting by connected-component size, while IPS performs top-fraction selection using mean proposal similarity. Connected components can merge neighboring instances through chaining, and cluster size is confounded by object scale, proposal density, and detector architecture; the reported weakness on small objects is consistent with this issue.

The entropy formulation applies a categorical softmax over foreground classes, whereas the evaluated detectors commonly use detector-specific sigmoid/token scores and explicit or implicit background/objectness mechanisms. The paper should justify this conversion and study sensitivity to the queried label set, since adding absent categories can change both entropy and predicted cluster membership.

Comparisons focus mostly on classification-oriented VLM adaptation methods reimplemented for detection. Dedicated object-detector TTA methods are discussed but not evaluated, and the larger-backbone study compares only against zero-shot inference. These omissions make it harder to establish the advantage over the strongest relevant alternatives.

The paper reports single aggregate results without confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics. Even if inference is largely deterministic, optimization, initialization, and prompt generation can introduce variance, and several gains on driving datasets are small enough that uncertainty would be informative.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper addresses a relevant and comparatively underexplored problem: efficient test-time adaptation of open-vocabulary vision-language detectors. The proposed use of proposal-overlap structure is well motivated for detection and distinguishes the work from classification-oriented TTA.

The two components are simple and technically plausible. IWE reweights entropy using class-consistent IoU connected components, while IPS selects image-compatible textual prompts. The formulation is easy to understand and can be incorporated into both CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: six domain-shift datasets, PASCAL-C and COCO-C corruptions, two detector families, larger-backbone experiments, multiple metrics, efficiency measurements, sensitivity studies, and qualitative analysis. VLOD-TTA consistently improves over zero-shot inference and the adapted TPT, VPT, DPE, and standard adapter baselines.

The main ablation supports both components: on the three style-shift datasets, IWE consistently improves over ordinary adapter entropy minimization, and IPS provides a further gain. Additional experiments with batch-normalization parameters and IoU-weighted pseudo-labeling suggest that the underlying weighting idea is not restricted to one adapter design or loss.

The paper provides a candid failure analysis. It identifies weak proposal overlap for small objects and rider/person confusion on Cityscapes, verifies these explanations through resolution and label-merging studies, and acknowledges the remaining test-time backpropagation cost.
weaknesses: The efficiency claims should be moderated. VLOD-TTA reduces YOLO-World throughput from 89 to 20 FPS and increases Grounding DINO latency from 210.6 to 531.6 ms/image, so it is substantially cheaper than TTAOD-F but not low-overhead relative to zero-shot inference. Moreover, the TTAOD-F comparison uses batch size 4 while VLOD-TTA uses batch size 1, confounding the reported memory and latency comparison; matched-batch timing and a precise accounting of all pre-update and post-update forward passes are needed.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript contains an empty “Code:” field, does not provide the complete generated prompt pools, and identifies the prompt generator only as “ChatGPT-5.” Important optimization details such as the optimizer, Grounding-DINO learning rate, default IoU threshold, detector thresholds, and exact update/inference sequence are absent or scattered. Since prompt generation and hyperparameters materially affect results, code and complete configurations are important.

The protocol for choosing hyperparameters is unclear. Several values are selected from sensitivity curves evaluated directly on the target style-shift datasets, and the text notes dataset-dependent optima. The paper should state what validation data or source-domain criterion was used without target labels and ideally report performance using a single configuration fixed before evaluating every target domain.

Evidence specifically isolating IPS is narrower than the overall benchmark. The component ablation is limited mainly to three related artistic datasets using YOLO-World, where IPS adds relatively modest gains over IWE. An IWE-only versus IWE+IPS comparison across Grounding DINO, driving, low-light, and corruption settings would establish whether IPS broadly contributes to the headline results.

IWE assumes that large connected components of same-predicted-class proposals are reliable. Connected components can grow through transitive IoU chains, favor large objects, merge nearby instances, and reinforce systematic class errors; the rider/person results demonstrate the latter failure mode. The paper offers useful examples and sensitivity plots but lacks aggregate analysis by object size, crowding, component purity, or false-positive cluster size.

No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis are reported. Even if per-image adaptation is mostly deterministic, results can depend on prompt generation, optimizer behavior, initialization, and implementation choices; this is especially relevant where improvements over the strongest baseline are small, such as 26.2 versus 26.0 mAP against TTAOD-F.

The proposed IoU-weighted entropy objective is simple, detection-specific, and intuitively exploits information discarded by classification-oriented TTA methods. The extension to IoU-weighted pseudo-labeling provides some evidence that the idea is not restricted to one loss.

Results are generally consistent across YOLO-World and Grounding DINO. The ablations examine component contributions, adapter placement, parameter subsets, prompt sources, input resolution, and several hyperparameters.

The paper candidly identifies important limitations, including weak proposal overlap for small objects, semantic confusion between rider and person, and substantial remaining latency relative to zero-shot inference.
The presentation is mostly clear, with useful diagrams and extensive supplementary results.
weaknesses: The empirical protocol does not establish how hyperparameters were chosen without target-label leakage. Sensitivity studies are conducted directly on the evaluated style-shift datasets, the text discusses dataset-dependent optima, and different detector-specific settings are used, but no source-only validation protocol is specified. This is especially consequential in test-time adaptation, where target labels should not inform method selection.

The comparison with TTAOD-F is materially confounded. TTAOD-F uses batch size 4 while the proposed method uses batch size 1; the paper acknowledges that changing the former to batch size 1 changes its accuracy. The warm-start variant additionally adopts a different initialization and test-stream assumption. Consequently, the claimed superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off is not demonstrated under matched conditions.

The claimed low-overhead framing is overstated. YOLO-World throughput falls from 89 to 20 FPS, while Grounding DINO latency rises from 210.6 to 531.6 ms/image and memory from 1.36 to 3.76 GB. These are substantial deployment costs despite being lower than TTAOD-F.

The main mechanism rests on a fragile heuristic: large connected components of same-predicted-class boxes are treated as reliable. Connected components can join proposals through transitive IoU chains, favor large objects or duplicate proposals, and reinforce systematic class errors. The paper itself reports severe rider/person degradation and reduced effectiveness for small objects, but provides no calibration, safeguards, or broad class/size-stratified analysis.

The formulation minimizes a foreground-class softmax entropy over detector proposals without clearly accounting for background/objectness. For thousands of mostly background proposals, sharpening an arbitrary foreground distribution can create confirmation bias. The exact interaction with the native scoring/objectness formulations of both YOLO-World and Grounding DINO is insufficiently specified.

IPS ranks each class's prompts using similarity averaged over all proposals, so background and frequent objects can dominate the image-conditioned score. The Euclidean-equivalence proposition is algebraically correct but does not justify why this global average identifies class-relevant prompts. A shared residual added to every prompt is also weakly motivated.

The ablations do not fully disentangle improvements from prompt ensembling, IPS, IWE, and adaptation. Table 3 only adds IPS on top of IWE; a complete factorial comparison under identical adapters and compute is absent. Figure 4's prompt-selection experiment does not clearly state whether adaptation and other components are controlled.

There is no uncertainty analysis, repeated-run variance, or significance testing. This matters because the advantage over TTAOD-F is only 0.2 average mAP in the default comparison and several gains over the Adapter baseline are modest.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the code link is blank, and central details such as the default IoU threshold, optimizer configuration, complete learning-rate protocol, exact checkpoints, score/NMS thresholds, dataset splits, and class mappings are missing or scattered. Reliance on unspecified ChatGPT-5 prompt generation further complicates exact reproduction.

There are internal reporting inconsistencies. For example, the paper claims the method is best on every PASCAL-C corruption, but DPE obtains 75.0 AP50 on Brightness versus 74.9 for the proposed method; ClipArt AP50 is reported as 45.4 in the main table and 45.2 in the supplementary fine-tuning table. These errors weaken confidence in the extensive tabulated results.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper has a useful idea and broad experiments, but the novelty is incremental and the unresolved protocol, fairness, and reproducibility issues prevent the evidence from supporting acceptance in its current form. A matched-baseline study and a label-independent model-selection protocol could substantially change the assessment.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relatively underexplored problem: efficient test-time adaptation of open-vocabulary vision-language object detectors. Under the default Algorithms/General category, the detection-specific treatment of test-time adaptation is a meaningful computer-vision contribution.

IoU-weighted entropy is simple, intuitive, and well motivated by the dense, overlapping proposal structure of detectors. The extension to IoU-weighted pseudo-labeling provides useful evidence that proposal-overlap weighting is broader than the particular entropy objective.

Image-conditioned prompt selection is a sensible alternative to indiscriminate prompt averaging. The component ablations show consistent incremental gains from IWE and IPS, and the prompt-generation and selection analyses help clarify when language prompts are useful.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: two substantially different detector families, multiple model sizes, artistic shifts, driving scenes, low-light and specialized underwater imagery, plus PASCAL-C and COCO-C across corruption types and severities. Improvements are generally consistent across mAP, AP50, and AP75.

The method compares favorably with the specialized TTAOD-F baseline on COCO-C, attaining slightly better average mAP with much lower memory and latency. It also consistently exceeds the strongest generic adapter baseline in the main experiments.

The supplementary analyses are valuable. They cover hyperparameter sensitivity, batch size, augmentations, adapter placement, input resolution, backbone scaling, pre-adaptation fine-tuning, and failure modes involving small objects and overlapping labels.

The paper is clearly organized and offers helpful qualitative examples. It candidly identifies limitations involving small objects, ambiguous classes, and test-time backpropagation rather than overstating universal effectiveness.
weaknesses: The core novelty is moderate: IWE is essentially connected-component-size reweighting of proposal entropy, while IPS ranks and averages prompt similarities. The contribution is compelling mainly through its detection-specific combination and extensive validation rather than a major algorithmic advance.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate. The manuscript shows an empty code link and omits or leaves unclear several consequential details in the main setup, including the default IoU threshold, optimizer and learning rate, detector thresholds, exact proposal handling, complete generated prompt pools, and detailed configurations of the adapted baselines.

The paper reports only single results, without repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Since many gains over the adapter baseline are modest—often below one mAP point—evidence about run-to-run stability would strengthen the case.

The TTAOD-F efficiency comparison is not fully controlled: TTAOD-F uses its original batch size of four while VLOD-TTA uses one, and the paper notes that changing the former affects accuracy. This makes the headline latency and memory comparison informative but not strictly apples-to-apples. The warm-start variant also needs a more explicit deployment protocol.

IWE can systematically favor large proposal clusters and suppress valid small or rare objects; its total influence grows more than linearly because every proposal in a component receives a component-size weight. The Cityscapes analysis confirms this limitation, but broader class-size-stratified evaluation would establish its practical severity.

Hyperparameter selection is insufficiently separated from evaluation. The supplement discusses dataset-dependent optima for IoU threshold, fusion weight, learning rate, and other choices, but does not clearly state which labeled data, if any, informed the final settings. This is particularly important in a source-free test-time setting.

Despite being described as low-overhead or suitable for real-time deployment, adaptation reduces YOLO-World throughput from 89 to 20 FPS and increases Grounding DINO latency from 210.6 to 531.6 ms/image. The method is efficient relative to several adaptation baselines, but not relative to zero-shot deployment, so the real-time framing should be qualified.

Theoretical support for IPS is limited to the elementary equivalence between average cosine similarity and average squared distance for normalized embeddings. This does not justify why averaging compatibility over thousands of mostly background proposals identifies the most semantically appropriate prompt, nor does the paper isolate robustness to proposal-background composition.
